newsitem.title: ITALY: Vatican says don't force couples to limit families.
newsitem.headline: Vatican says don't force couples to limit families.

text.p: The Vatican on Saturday told nations at the World Food Summit that food security aims could not be based on population controls that urged or forced people to limit the size of their families.

The Vatican said it was joining the overall consensus on the U.N.-sponsored summit's final document but requested that its reservations on some points and its interpretation of some terms become part of the record.

"The Holy See reasserts that the stabilisation of the world's population must not be achieved by national or international measures which deny the right of spouses to decide on procreation and the spacing of births," one of the Vatican's reservations said.

The Vatican has in the past accused some developed countries and international development agencies of making aid conditional on their acceptance of birth control programmes to stem their population growth.
It has also denounced countries which legally force couples to limit the size of their families.

Pope John Paul told the food summit on Wednesday that demography alone could not explain inadequate distribution of food resources and rejected as "sophistry" a view that "when there are many, one is condemned to be poor".

A day later the U.N's top population official, executive director Nafis Sadik of the U.N. Population Fund, contested the Pope's view, saying the world's future food needs would be inextricably linked to demographic changes.

The plan of action at the food summit adopts a passage from the 1994 Population Conference in Cairo which committed countries to promoting primary health care and reproductive health services for all, especially the poor, vulnerable and disadvantaged.
The Vatican and many developed countries clashed bitterly at the Cairo conference.
There, the issue of "reproductive rights" became a minefield because the Vatican felt the phrase was a backdoor way of supporting abortion as a means of controlling population growth.

The Vatican's reservation said references in the final document to family planning and reproductive health should not be seen as a change in the Roman Catholic Church's opposition to artificial birth control.
The Catholic Church permits only natural family planning methods.

In his address to the summit on Saturday, the Vatican's secretary of state, Cardinal Angelo Sodano, said giving food security to all people on all continents was not only a technical and economic challenge but an ethical one.
